Introduction/Organisation transformation

Development guide

Organisation transformation

Introducing AI tools changes more than how a team drafts code. Someone still needs to define the task, check the result and decide whether it can be used. When drafting becomes faster, unclear requirements or limited review capacity can become more visible.

This chapter helps product managers, team leads and delivery teams plan changes across people, process, culture and technology. Follow one upload-feature pilot, then use its evidence to decide what happens next. You can commission the technical checks without configuring the platform yourself.

Here, organisational transformation means changing how delivery teams and their shared services adopt AI-assisted development: using AI to support development work. You need familiarity with planning and review, rather than AI configuration. The resulting software does not need to contain AI.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Support learning
  • Prepare review evidence
  • Learn from failures
  • Test bounded delegation

Why the way of working needs to change

Faster drafting helps only if the team can turn the draft into useful, reliable software. Unclear requirements, unavailable reviewers and delayed release decisions can move the saving into another queue. Organisational transformation connects the new tool to the people and services needed to finish the work.

Start with one recurring delay or quality problem. Agree the intended improvement, arrange the supporting changes and run a small pilot before extending the workflow. Compare accepted results, waiting, review and correction effort, quality and cost.

What the research means for your team

External research gives reasons to examine the whole workflow; it does not predict your team's productivity gain. DORA describes AI as amplifying existing organisational strengths and weaknesses. Improving review capacity, clear instructions and reliable delivery services therefore belongs in the change plan alongside introducing tools. [1]

McKinsey found an association between reported AI value and workflow redesign. Its survey does not establish that redesign caused the results. METR's early-2025 experiment found slower completion for experienced developers in familiar open-source repositories; that finding applies to the studied tools, tasks and participants. Its February 2026 follow-up had selection and time-measurement problems, so it could not reliably estimate the current effect. [2] [3] [4]

Measure your own work from an agreed task brief to an accepted result. Count failed attempts and specialist review, and record elapsed time separately from active human effort. The research detail in Sources retains the figures and study context.

Four areas that change together

Training reviewers will not help if they have no time to review. Give them current requirements and a test environment, schedule the review and support them in raising a failed check. People, process, culture and technology describe these connected changes, rather than four separate projects.

  • People: who can specify, perform and review the task? Name participants, skill gaps and coaching time.
  • Process: what evidence supports progress, and who decides? Record the task flow, checks and decision authority.
  • Culture: how will people raise concerns and learn from failures? Agree a feedback route and review date.
  • Technology: what can the tool access, change and recover? Record access limits, action records and a recovery method.
Worked exampleFictional upload pilotStart with one change you can assessFollow one upload task from agreed boundaries to an adoption decision.

A team trials AI-assisted development on a document upload feature. An AI agent uses a model to choose or adapt actions and tool use towards a goal, within agreed permissions. Here, it may edit a separate working copy of the code, called a branch, and run tests using synthetic documents and simulated recipients.

The product owner agrees three expected behaviours before coding:

  • An allowed upload succeeds.
  • An unsupported file is rejected.
  • A recipient without permission cannot receive the document.

Before drafting, the platform engineer sets up the separate test storage and checks the branch permissions and recovery method. The team agrees to stop affected work on any unexpected access request or action outside the permitted scope. It wants to learn whether the agent reduces human effort without weakening the agreed checks. The feature itself does not contain AI. All events, dates and figures in this running example are fictional.

People: develop skills and organise responsibilities

AI-assisted work still needs people who can specify the user need and recognise an incorrect result. Arrange time to learn and review alongside implementation time. Existing professional expertise remains necessary when the tool produces the first draft.

Organise delegated work and review capacity

For each task, agree who defines the outcome, performs the work and reviews the result. Confirm what evidence each reviewer needs and who is authorised to accept the change. Assign work according to the team's capacity to check it; more agents or smaller teams are not measures of maturity.

For a consequential decision, ask reviewers to form an independent view before accepting an agent-supported recommendation. Compare the intended outcome with original tests or user observations, consider alternative explanations and record what remains uncertain. Tests generated from the same misunderstood requirement can repeat the implementation error.

Quality assurance (QA) assesses behaviour and reliability; security assesses threats and protective controls. Keep their findings and decision responsibilities distinct under the existing process. Functional acceptance, security approval and release permission remain separate decisions.

Learn through supported practice

Pair a learner with a coach on a low-risk task and include a deliberately flawed output. Before starting, agree which errors the learner should find and what evidence should support a correction. The coach records detected and missed errors, the learner's explanation and the next practice task. Finishing the task or attending a course alone does not demonstrate review competence.

Develop enough breadth to follow a user requirement across design, implementation and testing, while retaining specialist depth. This is often called a T-shaped skill profile. Use the role competency reference to choose a relevant development need, rather than expecting everyone to master every role.

Worked exampleFictional upload pilotReserve time for an independent reviewSee why delegating the draft changes the work people need to do.

The product owner and developer write the upload brief together. The team lead reserves time for the developer to inspect the result, a security reviewer to examine recipient access and a technical lead to review the integrated change. These are this fictional team's arrangements, mapped to its existing decision authorities.

The developer receives the agreed recipient rules before delegating the draft. The lead keeps specialist review time in the plan even though the agent is expected to draft faster. The next section shows what that review finds.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to draft alternative approaches to the practice task and state its assumptions. The learner and coach compare each approach with the agreed criteria, record errors and choose what to practise next. Assess the review as well as the finished work.

What you do as team lead

With each participant, choose one responsibility to practise and name a reviewer with time to assess it. Keep the practice criteria, observed gaps and coaching time in a skills-and-capacity plan.

Use that plan to decide which tasks the team can support. Ask specialists to assess work beyond the team's competence; completing training does not grant new acceptance or release authority.

Process: connect checks to decisions

Map how a task reaches an accepted result today. Separate time doing work from time waiting for information, review or approval. A slow checkpoint may need clearer inputs or more reviewer capacity.

  1. Ask the control owner what outcome the checkpoint protects.
  2. Agree the original results a reviewer needs, the criteria for judging them and the record to retain.
  3. Confirm who can authorise progress and where a failed check or missing evidence sends the work next.

A passing check supplies evidence for a decision. Record acceptance or rework with its reason, assessed revision and unresolved findings. An AI summary that says “passed” cannot replace a missing original result.

Agree what the agent may do

Choose permissions for the task's impact and reversibility. An advice-only task changes no system; an isolated task can edit a branch and run permitted tests. Routine actions need explicit prior scope and stop conditions. High-impact or uncertain actions need the applicable authorisation before execution. The task-boundary reference gives the detailed options and decision flow.

IMDA's agentic AI framework recommends assessing risks and bounding an agent's powers before use. It retains human accountability and meaningful oversight, supported by controls throughout the agent lifecycle. Apply those principles by naming the delegator, permitted actions, significant decision points and stop conditions in the task record. [5] [6]

Worked exampleFictional upload pilotTrace a failed check through correctionCompare expected and observed behaviour before accepting the revised result.

The agent drafts the upload change and its tests, but neither checks whether the selected recipient has permission. The developer compares both with the brief and reproduces the defect using a simulated unauthorised recipient. The first revision allows delivery; the expected result is denial.

The developer records the failure, corrects the instructions and asks the agent to revise the change. For the corrected revision, the retained record shows:

  • Unauthorised recipient: delivery is denied and no document is received, matching the access rule.
  • Authorised recipient: the permitted upload and delivery succeed.
  • Unsupported file: the upload is rejected with the expected explanation.

The record links the brief, both revisions, failed and passing results and review findings. The security reviewer checks the access evidence; the technical lead checks integration against the brief. They record no unresolved findings within this isolated scope. The authorised acceptance owner accepts the corrected test result; production release and wider access remain outside the pilot.

AIHow AI can help

Given the change, criteria and original test results, AI can assemble evidence links and flag apparent gaps. The control owner compares its summary with the original results, records missing or contradictory evidence and routes the findings to the authorised decision-maker.

What you do as team lead

Agree one checkpoint with its control owner. Keep a workflow record naming the input, expected evidence, failure route and person authorised to decide.

Use it to arrange review and rework. Refer exceptions and release requests to the existing authority; the lead's coordination role does not confer approval rights.

Culture: make learning and accountability visible

People need to be able to question AI output, report failures and ask for help without pressure to demonstrate speed gains. Explain the pilot's purpose and how responsibilities may change before starting. Record concerns about workload, job responsibilities and learning time, with an owner for unanswered questions.

DORA's guidance connects a high-trust culture and effective information flow with stronger performance. Its AI Capabilities Model also identifies clear communication about permitted AI use as a supporting capability. Make the approved tools, data limits and help route easy to find, then use reported problems to improve the workflow. [7] [8]

At a retrospective, compare the reported difficulty with the task instructions, tool actions and review results. Agree a specific improvement, owner and completion date. Recognise defects caught and useful escalation alongside completed work.

Worked exampleFictional upload pilotKeep the extra work visibleUse a reported failure to improve instructions and account for review effort.

The developer raises the recipient-access omission instead of reporting the first draft as complete. The team retains the failed result and the time spent diagnosing and correcting it. A quick draft is not counted as an accepted change.

The retrospective proposes a further change: ask the agent to list the required acceptance cases before drafting code. The developer prepares that instruction, and the security reviewer checks that the expected recipient denial is included before the next trial. The pilot lead includes every review round and rejected attempt in the effort comparison, so the failure remains visible when the team discusses benefits.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to group permitted feedback and failure reports into themes linked to the original records. Participants compare the themes with their accounts, correct omissions or contradictions and retain agreed improvements, owners and follow-up dates.

What you do as team lead

Invite concerns before starting and discuss one failed task with the people involved. Keep the concern, supporting record, agreed improvement, owner and due date in the team action log.

Use the follow-up to change instructions, workload or coaching. Route unresolved risk to its decision owner, and do not turn reported speed into a target that discourages disclosure.

Technology: provide bounded access and recovery

Start with existing repositories, test environments and delivery services. Ask specialists to demonstrate what the agent can access, what prevents an unauthorised action and how the team can stop and recover its work. A new platform is not a prerequisite.

The instructions, tools, permissions and checks surrounding an agent form its agent harness. In the upload pilot, this includes the task brief, branch-editing tools, test commands and access limits. Name who maintains that setup and which version the trial uses.

Ask for demonstrations you can use

  • Access and isolation: the platform and security owners show that the agent can use only the agreed data and environment. Retain evidence that an unauthorised action is denied.
  • Checks before progress: the platform engineer demonstrates that a failed required test blocks the next delivery step. Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) are the automated steps that build, test and prepare software for release; deployment still follows the applicable authority.
  • Stop and recovery: the platform and application owners demonstrate stopping a run, revoking access and restoring affected state. Record recovery results, actions that cannot be undone and the support contact.

OWASP recommends giving agents only the tools, permissions and autonomy needed for their task. Connected systems should enforce authorisation on each action. An instruction in a prompt cannot substitute for those access controls. [9]

Keep verification independent of generation: an agent's claim that its work is correct is not independent evidence. If AI assesses results, ask the check owner to compare it with qualified reviewers using agreed cases and error criteria. A missed critical defect cannot be cancelled out by high overall agreement. The platform reference explains assessment, infrastructure and operational checks.

Worked exampleFictional upload pilotDemonstrate the pilot boundarySee the difference between testing generated code and controlling what the agent can do.

Before the adoption review, the platform engineer rechecks the boundary used throughout the pilot: separate test storage, the upload branch and synthetic data. In an agreed permission test, merge and production-deployment requests are denied. These results assess the agent's authority; the recipient tests assess the generated feature's behaviour.

The engineer also repeats the demonstration of stopping a run, revoking its test access and restoring the test state. The pilot record retains these results with the harness revision and a support contact. The corrected feature tests do not widen those permissions.

AIHow AI can help

An agent can draft code and run permitted tests on the isolated task. Developers inspect the changes against the brief; platform and security specialists test permissions and recovery. Retain their original results before proposing a wider scope.

What you do as team lead

Commission the demonstrations from the system, platform and security owners. Keep a short readiness record with tested permissions, blocked actions, recovery results, versions and support contacts.

Use the findings to propose a supported pilot scope. Specialists judge the technical controls and the applicable authority grants permissions; the lead does not infer access rights from passing feature tests.

Ownership: maintain shared capabilities

A squad pilot depends on services that someone must continue to maintain. Confirm who supports the agent setup, delivery environment and approved model service; who handles an incident; and who funds maintenance and support. Map those responsibilities to existing owners with capacity and a deputy or help route.

Keep contacts, capacity, funding gaps and review dates with the service documentation. Leads report gaps; service owners communicate changes and known limits. The shared service ownership reference retains the full maintenance matrix. A pilot lead does not automatically become the platform owner.

Evaluation cases are sample tasks with expected results used to assess a tool against agreed criteria. For this pilot, they include generating the upload change and checking whether reviewers find the omitted recipient rule. Keep these assessments of the development tool separate from tests of the feature. If the delivered product contains AI, its behaviour also needs an evaluation and monitoring owner.

Next step: agree an ownership record with the relevant service and budget owners. Resolve unsupported capabilities or funding gaps before proposing wider adoption; retain the isolated pilot boundaries until the authorised owner changes them.

Run a pilot and decide from evidence

A pilot is a small trial of a proposed way of working. Choose a recurring task whose result you can check and whose failures the team can contain and recover from. Name a pilot lead to collect results and confirm who can decide adoption.

  1. Record the baseline. Collect comparable recent task records, from agreed brief to acceptance. Include waiting, human effort, defects and cost.
  2. Agree the boundaries. Record task types, tool and harness versions, data, permissions, reviewers and stop conditions. For a running service, name responders and demonstrate alerting and recovery before starting.
  3. Set targets before the trial. Agree task counts, quality and control criteria, effort and cost targets, and the period for observing defects after acceptance. Confirm separate functional, security and adoption authorities.
  4. Record every attempt. Include rejected and abandoned work, recovery and repeated reviews. Keep original results and ask participants about extra work and support needs.
  5. Compare and decide. Present baseline and trial results with evidence links and gaps. Record the decision, supported scope, follow-up owners and next review date.

Use the same definitions in both periods and compare similar tasks separately. Explain differences in risk, difficulty and repository experience. Mark missing evidence as unknown: a small before-and-after comparison can inform the next decision without showing that AI caused the difference. Use the full scorecard reference to prepare the record.

Worked exampleFictional upload pilotCount all effort before decidingSee why a faster draft can still miss the adoption target.

The pilot lead compares small upload-related changes in the same repository, with the same team, acceptance criteria and agreed size and risk band. The team also gains experience during the trial, so this comparison does not isolate AI's effect. The baseline covers 8–19 September 2026; the AI-assisted trial covers 22 September–3 October. Each accepted change is observed for 14 calendar days, ending by 17 October. The authorised adoption owner reviews the record on 19 October.

The agreed effort target is at least 15 fewer human minutes per accepted change: no more than 75 minutes against the 90-minute baseline. The team also requires all three agreed behaviours to pass on accepted revisions, no unresolved access-control failure and no critical defect during follow-up. An effort saving cannot offset a failed control.

Worked effort comparison

The baseline has seven task attempts: six accepted changes and one abandoned attempt. The trial has eight: six accepted changes and two abandoned attempts. Revisions to the same attempt stay within that attempt's record. All task effort, including abandoned work, is divided by the six accepted changes in each period.

Human task effort per accepted change — fictional minutes
ActivityBaselineAI-assisted trial
Draft the change60 minutes20 minutes
Review20 minutes50 minutes
Correct and recheck10 minutes20 minutes
Total human task effort90 minutes90 minutes

The underlying baseline totals are 360 drafting, 120 review and 60 correction minutes: 540 ÷ 6 = 90. Trial totals are 120, 300 and 120 minutes: also 540 ÷ 6 = 90. Drafting includes brief preparation and agent instructions; review includes specialist review of each submitted revision; correction includes fixes and rerunning checks after rejection. The pilot lead assigns each person's time once to an activity. Simultaneous work by two people counts as two people's effort.

The effort target was missed. The 40-minute drafting saving was absorbed by 30 more review minutes and 10 more correction minutes. These are active task-effort figures, excluding waiting and shared setup or training. They cannot establish a reduction in elapsed time or total cost.

Complete the rest of the scorecard

  • Accepted results and usefulness: six changes in each period meet the isolated test criteria after correction. No evidence of usefulness in live use was collected; user benefit remains unknown.
  • Elapsed time: task start and acceptance timestamps were not consistently retained. The baseline/trial comparison is unknown.
  • Quality follow-up: zero defects were recorded for the six baseline and six trial accepted changes during each change's 14-day isolated-test observation. No required recipient check remains unresolved on the accepted revisions. This small synthetic-data observation does not establish production quality.
  • Controls and support: the trial's branch, merge and deployment boundaries and recovery demonstration passed; the platform owner retained the results and support contact. Baseline permission and recovery results were not collected in a comparable form. Live-service readiness remains unassessed.
  • Total cost: shared setup, training, support allocation and complete tool charges were not recorded. Total cost and cost per accepted result are unknown for both periods.
  • Participant experience: four respondents—the product owner, developer, security reviewer and technical lead—report that review took more attention than expected. Platform feedback was not collected. No comparable baseline feedback was collected; the pilot lead retains the comments without claiming an improvement.

Completed decision record: keep testing

On 19 October, the authorised adoption owner decides Keep testing, with no expansion. The record links the task brief, attempt log, harness revision, original tests, specialist reviews, effort totals and participant comments. It records the missed effort target, unknown cost and elapsed time, and the absence of live-use evidence.

The owner permits a further trial of six task attempts, ending 30 October, to test whether listing the acceptance cases before drafting reduces review effort. It keeps the same branch-only permissions and synthetic data. The developer updates the instructions; the security reviewer checks the expected denial case; the pilot lead records every attempt, complete timestamps, setup and training effort, charges and comparable participant feedback. The platform owner confirms support and the existing stop conditions.

Each accepted result receives the same 14-day follow-up, ending by 13 November. The adoption owner reviews the full scorecard on 16 November against the unchanged effort target and required checks. If evidence is still missing, expansion remains unsupported. A revised isolated test still cannot authorise production deployment or wider data access.

Decide whether to expand, restrict, stop or keep testing

Agree these suggested rules before starting. The decision owner records the evidence, supported uses and remaining uncertainty; greater autonomy is not a success measure.

  • Expand when outcomes, quality, total cost and participant experience meet the agreed criteria, required controls pass and defect follow-up is complete. Confirm funding, ownership and reviewer capacity. Extend only to supported tasks and permissions.
  • Restrict when benefits hold for some tasks but other tasks create excessive review effort, defects or failed checks. Narrow tasks or permissions, restore human checks where needed and repeat the relevant evaluation before restoring excluded uses.
  • Stop when evaluated revisions repeatedly miss targets, a required control cannot be maintained, or ongoing cost and support outweigh the benefit. The authorised owner ends the use, removes its access and returns the work to a supported workflow.
  • Keep testing when a specific question remains, such as weak comparison, incomplete follow-up or a revision needing evaluation. Retain the existing limits, assign the additional work and set an end date.

If a stop condition occurs during the trial, stop the affected actions immediately and follow the agreed response and recovery procedure. Reassess after a material model, harness or workflow change. Do not let a pilot continue indefinitely without a new evidence question and end date.

AIHow AI can help

AI can draft the comparison from the attempt records and agreed measure definitions. The pilot lead checks denominators, totals, repeated reviews, abandoned work and missing evidence against the original records. Retain the corrected comparison for the authorised adoption decision.

Next step: prepare a short pilot brief with the task, participants, baseline, boundaries, success criteria, evidence owners and review date. Ask the existing decision owner to agree the proposed scope. Use the Concepts guide for ways to specify and supervise the work.

Delivery reference: roles, controls and measurement

Use these optional references with specialists when preparing a pilot or commissioning evidence. The main chapter explains the decisions; these tables retain the detailed responsibilities and checks.

Role competencies, skill breadth and accountable delegation

The role examples help participants agree development needs; assess competence through observed decisions and reviewed work. Here, “product owner” means the person clarifying user need, scope and acceptance criteria. Where product management and ownership are separate, agree their contributions under the existing process. A business analyst's contribution does not grant acceptance authority.

For interface work, design tokens are named values for colour, typography and spacing. A designer could supply these for the upload form so generated screens follow the agreed design. They guide presentation; they do not test recipient permissions.

Prompt injection is an attempt to redirect an agent using instructions in untrusted content. For an upload-development task, a synthetic document could contain text asking the agent to ignore its brief; the security reviewer can use that case to test the boundary. The current pilot does not grant access to real uploaded documents.

Evaluation cases assess the development tool using representative tasks and expected outcomes. Maintain ordinary and deliberately difficult cases, including a missing recipient rule, so overall success cannot hide a critical failure.

Include platform engineering capacity from planning through operation, within the squad or through a named shared team. Developers add application health signals and diagnose code failures; platform engineers maintain delivery and monitoring foundations. QA checks behaviour and reliability; security reviews threats and controls. Release and risk decisions follow existing authorities.

Multi-agent orchestration coordinates dependent or parallel tasks across several agents, then integrates their results. If several agents divided upload implementation and tests, a named person would still need to integrate and independently review both against the brief. This pilot uses one agent; orchestration remains an optional specialism with time for review and recovery.

The delegation diagram uses product owner (PO), business analyst (BA), technical lead, developer, platform engineer, QA and security reviewer as example contributors. Choose the task owner and reviewers according to the work and review capacity; it is not a staffing ratio.

The PRD and TRD guidance explains the product requirements document, which describes required outcomes, and technical requirements document, which records how the system will deliver them. Preparation and approval depend on the applicable workflow. Follow the Eitri planning steps when using that implementation.

Code review covers evidence for code changes. Data access, deployment and external communications need controls at their own execution points, including when they occur outside a merge request.

Platform checks, AI assessments, infrastructure and operations
Suggested capabilities and how to check them
CapabilityPractical check
Relevant contextGive the tool current requirements and approved reference material; record their versions and restrict access to what the task needs.

Assess an automated reviewer before relying on it

The check owner selects routine and higher-risk cases within the proposed task scope and agrees acceptable errors before testing. Qualified reviewers assess the original evidence against the same criteria, independently of the AI assessment. Compare missed defects, unsupported findings and unresolved disagreements; retain cases, versions, expected and observed results, reviewer findings and the suitability decision.

Permit only the use supported by those criteria. If the automated reviewer misses the required recipient-access defect, a high overall agreement rate does not make it suitable for that check. Keep specialist review or restrict the automated use while the defect is investigated.

DORA associates useful internal platforms and access to relevant internal data with stronger AI benefits. Improve context and platform quality while retaining task-specific access limits. [8]

Build, harden and operate the delivery path

  • CI/CD pipelines: maintain repeatable builds, tests, security checks and deployment stages, with task-limited credentials and retained results. Demonstrate that a failed check blocks progress and rehearse rollback. Follow the EDS pipeline stages when applying that workflow.
  • Infrastructure as code: describe resources and configuration in reviewed, version-controlled files. In the upload pilot, these could describe the separate test storage and its access settings. Infrastructure hardening means reducing exposure through agreed identity, network, secrets and patching controls. Retain checks, detect configuration drift from the agreed state and test restoration from backups where needed.
  • Operations and application health: developers and platform engineers collect metrics, logs and traces and check important user journeys. Agree service health targets for availability, latency, errors and resource capacity. Test alerts to a named responder and maintain diagnosis, escalation and recovery instructions.

AI can draft pipeline definitions, infrastructure changes and runbooks. Review generated changes and test them in isolation before authorised promotion. Agree separately who can deploy, change production infrastructure and respond to incidents. This guide maps practices to suggested contributors; actual ownership follows local operating arrangements.

Full pilot scorecard and evidence collection
Suggested pilot scorecard: agree targets before the trial
MeasureWhat to record and check
Tasks comparedDescribe the scope, difficulty and risk of each task type, participants’ experience and familiarity with the repository. Count baseline and trial attempts, including failures, and explain any differences that weaken the comparison.
Useful resultsRecord which results met the acceptance criteria and what shows they helped the intended user. Keep links to tests, review findings or user observations.
Time to an accepted resultMeasure elapsed time from the agreed start to acceptance, including waiting. Record active human effort separately so that a shorter wait is not mistaken for less work.
Review effortRecord time spent checking requirements, generated work and test evidence. Include specialist reviews and repeated review rounds.
Corrections and failed attemptsRecord time spent fixing rejected outputs, rerunning the tool and recovering from failures. Include effort spent on work that never reached acceptance.
Defects and control failuresTrack defects found after acceptance over the agreed observation period. Record severity, user impact, failed security or other required checks, incidents and recovery results. Examine each serious failure individually.
Readiness to run and support the serviceFor changes affecting delivery or a running service, record pipeline failures, infrastructure security findings, availability, response times and errors. Compare alert response and recovery results with agreed targets. Name the operational owner and record gaps before expanding.
Total costInclude tool and model charges, infrastructure, pipeline and monitoring services, setup, training, human work, shared harness maintenance, evaluation, support and incidents. Include failed attempts and count each cost once. Report both total cost and cost per accepted result.
Participants’ experienceAsk about mental effort, interruptions, learning and confidence in questioning AI output. Compare feedback with observed work and requests for help; fewer reported problems may mean problems went unnoticed.

Keep denominators and periods with each result. Divide all included task effort, including abandoned attempts, by accepted results. Count each person's effort once, retain total cost separately and do not infer a cash saving or shorter waiting time from an effort change alone.

Research detail behind the takeaways

McKinsey's November 2025 survey found its AI high-performer group nearly three times as likely as others to report fundamental workflow redesign. That group reported significant AI value and an AI contribution of at least 5% to earnings before interest and taxes. These self-reported associations do not establish causation or predict a delivery team's results. [2]

METR's early-2025 randomised study involved 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 tasks in familiar repositories. Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%, despite participants estimating that it saved time. This is a historical result for those tools, tasks and participants. In February 2026, METR reported selection effects and time-measurement problems that made follow-up data unreliable for estimating current productivity gains. Neither supplies a forecast for your team. [3] [4]
